newsitem.title: UK: Oil pressured by spectre of more Iraqi barrels.
newsitem.headline: Oil pressured by spectre of more Iraqi barrels.

text.p: World oil prices came under pressure on Wednesday as reports that United Nations officials are mulling an increase in Iraq's oil export quota sent a bearish shiver down traders' spines.

U.N. overseers are considering an allowance for Iraqi spot sales over and above the original export contracts signed under the U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food agreement to compensate for plummeting oil prices.
Benchmark North Sea Brent March futures in London were trading 10 cents down at $21.04 a barrel at 1608 GMT.
Brent prices have fallen rapidly from a post Gulf-War high of over $25 a barrel posted in early October.

As a result, a U.N. report filed last week put the total value of the first three-month's worth of Iraqi sales contracts at about $800 million, against a cash target of $1 billion for the first tranche of sales.

If the U.N. gives the go-ahead, international oil markets could be asked to soak up millions of extra barrels of crude to make up for the $200 million shortfall in Iraqi revenues for the first 90-day period.
"Any extra Iraqi oil will inevitably be bearish," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust in London.
If additional exports are sanctioned, they are likely to be in the form of one-off spot market sales rather than new term contracts, said a western diplomat close to the U.N.-Iraq deal.

"The overseers are keeping an eye on the oil price, and will make a recommendation on how to proceed at some point. Current prices are quite a bit under the $1 billion, and since that last report prices have come down more," he said.
Meanwhile, oil companies with contracts for the second 90 day period, which also carries a $1 billion sales target, are seeking to up to top-up volumes.
Traders' bearish sentiment was also reinforced on Wednesday by the release of weekly U.S. inventory data which showed a significant build in crude stocks.
"The (stocks data) was on the surface bearish, but much of the negative news was already discounted into the price of the market," said Charles Gray of Prudential Bache futures brokers in London.
Figures from the American Petroleum Institute showed a 3.64 million barrel build in crude oil stocks, while the Energy Information Administration estimated a increase of 3.5 million barrels.

A build in gasoline stocks of between three and five million tonnes also weighed on the market, but this was partly countered by a draw on distillate -- heating oil and diesel -- stocks of some five million barrels.
